summary: FIREFIRM turns NASA satellite fire detections into tools for scientists and firefighters. MODIS (2001 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward) count fires differently, so long-term records show a false jump in 2012. We trained a LightGBM model that converts MODIS counts into VIIRS S-NPP-equivalent counts, giving one continuous monthly fire calendar for 2001-2024 across six countries: Angola, Argentina, Brazil, Canada, the US, and Australia. On a held-out test set, it cut the error (Poisson deviance) from 5.17 for a simple multiplier to 1.09. Scientists can explore the calendar and download it. For firefighters, the site tracks watch points using live VIIRS NOAA-20/21 detections and each region’s fire season. It also runs a physics-based (Rothermel) fire spread simulator in the browser, driven by live weather forecasts and terrain. Spread is shown as a probability from 25 simulations, not a single line. The core features run in the user’s browser, so the site is free to use.
details:
Features

This web application has three modes: Scientist, Firefighter, and Simulator.

Scientist Mode
This mode is built for scientists. They can use the data for research, to build AI models, or as a tool for analysis and visualization. It includes:

  • FIRMS Calendar: A monthly fire calendar for 2001-2024 on an H3 grid across four regions. Users can switch between three series: Harmonized, raw MODIS, and measured VIIRS. Values back-cast from MODIS are hatched, so users can tell estimated values from measured ones, and show an ~80% uncertainty range. Months above the 90th percentile of the same month in 2013-2024 are marked as critical months. Users can select any area and period, then download the calendar (all three series in one CSV) or the raw FIRMS hotspots.
  • Evidence: Charts showing the 2012 seam between MODIS and VIIRS before and after harmonization, test scores by region, and every known limitation (for example, the largest fire months are underestimated).
  • AI Harmonization Model: A LightGBM model (Tweedie objective, 37 features such as FRP, brightness temperature, day/night, how often each sensor viewed the cell, Terra/Aqua share, and land cover) learned how MODIS counts relate to VIIRS S-NPP counts where both exist, then reconstructed 2001-2011. It was tested on areas and a year it had never seen. A separate model covers the Terra-only period before July 2002. The website shows these precomputed results; it does not forecast fire risk.

Firefighter Mode
This mode is built for firefighters. It helps them make decisions and monitor fires efficiently, in both urban and forest areas. It includes:

  • Watch Points: Locations with frequent past fires, chosen by our team. Each point shows a level. Active means VIIRS NOAA-20/21 detected a hotspot within the point's radius in the last 48 hours (low-confidence detections are excluded). High, Elevated, or Normal is set by comparing the current month with the region's fire season. These are simple, explainable rules, not fire probabilities. Each point also shows its own monthly fire history (median for 2013-2024).
  • Email Alerts: Firefighters can follow watch points. The alert service will check followed points every 3 hours and send an email only when a point's level rises (for example, from Elevated to Active), with the hotspot count, peak FRP, UTC time, and a one-click unsubscribe link. Sign-up uses a confirmation email (double opt-in). Status: the website side is complete. In the current demo, follows are saved in the browser and no email is sent yet; the email server is in development.
  • Fire Spread Forecast: Click an ignition point, then choose a fuel model and forecast length. Fire spread uses the Rothermel (1972) surface fire model with Albini's (1976) revisions and the Anderson 13 fuel models. Wind and slope are combined as vectors, and spread rate is capped at wind speed (Andrews et al. 2013). A minimum-travel-time solver runs on a 201x201 grid with hourly wind, temperature, and humidity from Open-Meteo, dead fuel moisture estimated from the past 24 hours, and slope from AWS Terrain Tiles. It runs 25 simulations with perturbed wind direction, wind speed, and fuel moisture, and maps the probability of fire reaching each cell or the fire arrival time. A forecast takes about 2 seconds in the browser.
  • Fire Simulator (Simulator mode): Set your own weather, draw firebreaks, and watch the fire spread in 3D on satellite imagery, with flame height from Byram’s flame length. Canopy height from Meta & WRI’s 1 m canopy height map is used for wind sheltering and crown fire (Van Wagner 1977, Rothermel 1991). This is useful for firefighting planning and education.
  • Limitations: Each simulation uses one fuel type for the whole area. In published studies, Rothermel’s spread rate has a median error of about 57% against real fires. Results are for planning, not for evacuation decisions.

Benefits

For scientists and firefighters

  • Support learning and long-term analysis with historical data from 2001 to 2024, enough to build models
  • Make research easier
  • Compare past and recent data
  • Plan seasonal planting
  • Plan firefighting strategies
  • Monitor fire risk areas

For the general public

  • Follow fire incidents
  • Free and open for everyone to access and use
  • Check long-term historical records

tech stack

website

  • programming language : typescript
  • framework : React 19 + Vite 8 + Tailwind CSS v4, React Router, TanStack Query
  • in-browser data and maps : DuckDB-WASM (queries Parquet files in the browser), MapLibre GL, terra-draw, Web Workers
  • testing : Vitest

ai back end

  • programming language : python + typescript
  • framework : express.js (watch point API), FastAPI (data API, built but not yet deployed) 
  • ai model : LightGBM (Python, Polars, DuckDB); data files hosted on a Hugging Face bucket

server

  • cloud : AWS EC2 server
  • tool : docker, nginx
  • dns provider : cloudflare
